title: The Disappearing Overnight Drift
one_line: The 2-3am ET ES drift that earned ~3.7%/yr in 1998-2020 has averaged close to zero in 2021-2025 (also NQ and YM); the authors trace it to closing order imbalances becoming much less dispersed.

findings.statement: The 2:00-3:00 am ET window earned ~3.7% a year (more than 60% of ES's 5.9% close-to-close return) in 1998-2020, and close to zero since 2021.
findings.evidence: Post-publication sample Jan 2021-Dec 2025, 1,245 trading days; same in NQ and YM.

findings.statement: The dispersion of closing order imbalances fell by more than half.
findings.evidence: SD of end-of-day relative signed volume 6.5% → 2.9%; VIX mean 20.4 → 19.4; overnight share of volume 15% → 16%.

findings.statement: The closing-imbalance → overnight-return link is much weaker in 2021-25.
findings.evidence: Spread between imbalance-sorted return bins much narrower.

findings.statement: NightShares overnight ETFs (NSPY, NIWM), launched June 2022, closed after ~14 months.
findings.evidence: Authors call this consistent with the weakened pattern (ETF costs also played a part).

why.pattern: Inventory risk premium that depends on closing imbalances; it fades when any of imbalance dispersion, variance or dealer capacity collapses.
why.mechanism: Closing limit orders became smaller (finer algorithmic slicing), so dealers carry less overnight inventory and earn less premium.
why.what_would_kill_it: Already weakened; it could return if closing-imbalance dispersion widens again (authors' prediction).

tradable_edge: Not a strategy on its own — a kill/regime switch for any overnight-drift strategy: trade the European-open long only when closing-imbalance proxies are large (e.g. a big last-30-minute move), otherwise stay flat.
angles: Regime switch: trade overnight long only after days with an unusually large last-30-minute move (imbalance proxy)
data_fit: ES 1-min (ETH + RTH) Dec 2013 → Sep 2026 in clean_ES_master.parquet; NQ 1-min Jul 2021 → Sep 2026. 2024+ is protected in the backtest project. Our ES data covers both regimes (2014-2020 vs 2021-2023 in development).
caveats: Authors' blog summary of the SSRN paper; full PDF not reached.
